name: DE Rantau Nomad Pass

requirements.blocker_text: Requires at least USD 24,000/year in income from foreign-based clients or employers, for tech and digital-economy roles (software engineering, cybersecurity, AI/blockchain development, digital content creation, data analysis, digital marketing).
requirements.fix_path: Document at least USD 24,000/year in verifiable foreign-sourced income.

requirements.blocker_text: Requires at least USD 60,000/year in income, for a broadened category of non-tech senior business and specialist roles (CEOs, CFOs, tax specialists, legal counsel, and similar) added to the programme in June 2024.
requirements.fix_path: Document at least USD 60,000/year in verifiable foreign-sourced income.

evidence_required.document: Active contracts, purchase orders, or invoices from foreign clients/employers showing contract duration and value
Health insurance valid for the full stay, explicitly covering treatment in Malaysia
MDEC online application, processed 6-8 weeks; RM 1,080 application fee (RM 540 per dependant)

outcome.duration_length: up to 12 months, renewable once for a maximum of 24 months total

notes: STATUS: DRAFT. HONEST SOURCING GAP: no direct fetch of the MDEC (Malaysia Digital Economy Corporation) official portal or FAQ was achieved in this research pass -- both sources here cite the official MDEC FAQ but were not independently verified against a directly-fetched government page. STRUCTURAL FINDING worth flagging: DE Rantau is legally structured as a variant of the Professional Visit Pass rather than a standalone visa category -- MDEC endorses the applicant, who then applies for the Professional Visit Pass itself through the Immigration Department, a two-step process. work_rights is 'restricted' rather than 'full': the entire premise is that the holder works exclusively for non-Malaysian clients/employers, and taking on Malaysian clients or employment is explicitly prohibited and grounds for pass revocation plus a re-entry ban -- similar in structure to Poland's and Brazil's digital-nomad routes documented elsewhere in this dataset, but with a notably harsher stated enforcement consequence (re-entry ban) than most. Malaysia offers a genuinely favourable tax treatment confirmed across multiple sources: foreign-sourced income is generally exempt from Malaysian tax under the Income Tax Act 1967 as administered by LHDN (the Inland Revenue Board), though freelancers invoicing Malaysian clients face a 10% withholding tax for the first 182 days -- a detail worth surfacing since it distinguishes purely-foreign-sourced nomads from those with any Malaysian client relationships. DE Rantau holders have no access to Malaysia's public healthcare system, unlike Employment Pass or MM2H holders in some tiers -- private health insurance is a hard requirement, not merely recommended.
